title: Comment from Steven Singleton
printtext:
Opening a dedicated comment window on the environmental assessment before any substantive rule is proposed gives the public an early opportunity to flag environmental concerns, which is a sound practice worth preserving as this petition moves forward.

The notice's principal shortcoming is that it does not disclose the substance of what CAP 5C0339 actually proposes. It states that the petition would add heavy metal limits and secondary names for carrot oil, but the notice includes no numeric limits and no proposed names. A member of the public reading only the Federal Register text cannot evaluate whether the proposed heavy metal limits are appropriately protective, because the limits themselves are not stated. FDA should include the specific proposed limits and names in the notice, or in an easily accessible summary alongside the docket, so that the comment period is meaningful to readers who do not separately visit the Dockets Management Staff office.

A second gap is that the notice does not summarize the environmental assessment's findings regarding acetone as a solvent in carrot oil manufacture, including whether the assessment addresses residual solvent levels in the finished color additive reaching food products. Acetone residue is a food-safety-adjacent question distinct from the environmental-impact question the current comment period is limited to; FDA should clarify whether safety data on residual acetone levels will be part of the record reviewed before any proposed rule, and if so, when that data will be made public.

Finally, FDA reserves authority to "consider other changes to the regulation, as appropriate, during the course of our review," without stating what triggers or bounds such additional changes. Some indication of the criteria FDA would use to add scope beyond the petition as filed would help commenters anticipate what a resulting proposed rule might cover.

These points concern the notice's transparency and scope, not the petition's merits, which cannot be evaluated without the missing detail.

Supplemental Comment
Americans for Scientific Integrity submits this supplemental comment to bring FDA’s attention to a recently accepted peer-reviewed study that further strengthens the biological plausibility underlying AFSI’s pending citizen petition regarding pediatric acetaminophen use.
The attached study, Sex-dependent effects of early-life paracetamol exposure on behavior and monoamines in the rat central nervous system (Górawski et al., Chemico-Biological Interactions, accepted January 2026), evaluates prenatal and early postnatal acetaminophen exposure in rodents and reports sex-dependent behavioral and neurochemical effects, with male and female offspring exhibiting different patterns of impact across behavioral domains and brain regions
Importantly, the findings do not reflect nonspecific or random neurotoxicity. Rather, the presence of systematic, sex-dependent differences suggests a biologically mediated effect consistent with known differences in neurodevelopment, hormone signaling, metabolism, and neurotransmitter systems between males and females. This pattern strengthens biological plausibility by arguing against chance injury and in favor of a drug-related developmental mechanism.
These sex-dependent findings align with observations in humans, where neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism spectrum disorder and ADHD are known to differ by sex in prevalence, presentation, and developmental trajectory. As such, this study adds relevant and timely preclinical evidence supporting AFSI’s request that FDA evaluate the need for precautionary labeling regarding pediatric acetaminophen use.
ASFI respectfully requests that FDA include this newly published study in its review and analysis of AFSI’s petition.

The comment addresses a broader safety concern: acetaminophen safety has historically been evaluated primarily through the lens of hepatic toxicity, but a growing body of evidence raises concern for possible non-hepatic effects, including reproductive and fertility-related endpoints, asthma/allergy associations, developing lung injury signals, and neurologic/dementia-related associations.

title: Comment from Anonymous
printtext:
I am a board certified anesthesiologist practicing in the United States. I am submitting this comment in strong support of the Americans for Scientific Integrity citizen petition requesting that FDA add a pediatric warning to acetaminophen products.

From a pharmacology and drug safety perspective, what concerns me most is not a subtle scientific nuance. It is the simple fact that acetaminophen was effectively grandfathered into widespread pediatric use on the basis of safety testing that focused almost entirely on acute liver injury. We validated dosing for hepatotoxicity. We did not meaningfully evaluate this drug for long term effects on the developing brain or on other organ systems in early life.

To my knowledge, the first animal studies that looked specifically at neurodevelopment in the context of early life acetaminophen exposure appeared only about a decade ago. Those data, summarized in the Americans for Scientific Integrity petition, are deeply concerning. They show behavioral and neurochemical changes after early life exposure that are consistent with injury to the developing nervous system. At the same time, human epidemiologic studies now repeatedly associate prenatal and early childhood acetaminophen exposure with increased risk of autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, and related neurodevelopmental outcomes. None of these signals existed when acetaminophen was informally “grandfathered” into pediatric practice. They exist now.

If we apply first principles and imagine that acetaminophen were a completely new drug being brought to FDA today, with the same preclinical neurodevelopmental findings and the same pattern of observational human data described in the petition, I do not believe it would clear even the early regulatory hurdles for pediatric use. In fact, I doubt the agency would allow clinical trials in infants or pregnant women to proceed in the face of these signals. Exposing a large number of children in a controlled trial to further characterize the risk would almost certainly be considered unethical, precisely because we already have evidence of possible harm.

That logic leads to an uncomfortable but inescapable conclusion. We are in a situation where the totality of the existing data is troubling enough that we probably could not ethically design the very studies that would be required to approve this drug for pediatric use if we were starting from scratch. Yet at the same time, more than 90 percent of children in early childhood receive acetaminophen, often repeatedly, sometimes in the exact age window where the petition argues susceptibility is highest. A drug that would struggle to obtain approval for pediatric trials under current standards is being used casually by nearly every family in the country, without any warning to parents that neurodevelopmental safety has never been adequately established.

The FDA cannot undo the regulatory and cultural decisions of the past. However, it can acknowledge where the evidence has moved and take corrective steps to protect children going forward. The fact that it is difficult to accept that a familiar, trusted over the counter drug might play a role in the autism epidemic does not change the ethical analysis. Our regulatory decisions should follow the evidence and the precautionary principle, not our discomfort.

In my judgment, based on the evidence compiled in the Americans for Scientific Integrity petition, acetaminophen could not be introduced today as a new pediatric analgesic and antipyretic without extensive additional safety work in neurodevelopmental models and careful limitation of any pediatric clinical trials. It is hard to imagine that such trials would even be approved given what we already know. If it is not ethical to expose children in a randomized trial under present knowledge, it is difficult to justify continuing unlabelled mass exposure in routine clinical practice.

For these reasons, I urge the agency to grant the petition’s request for a clear pediatric warning. At a minimum, parents and clinicians should be informed that:

Historical safety testing of acetaminophen focused primarily on acute liver toxicity, not neurodevelopment.

Neurodevelopmental safety in pregnancy and early childhood has never been robustly established.

Multiple animal and human studies now raise serious concerns, even though causation has not been definitively proven.

The FDA cannot change the past decisions that allowed acetaminophen to become embedded in pediatric care. It can, however, change the future by ensuring that parents are told the truth about the limitations of the safety data and about the concerning signals that now exist. Failing to provide at least a warning, given what we know today, would in my view be inconsistent with the agency’s duty to protect the public, especially infants and young children in the most vulnerable period of brain development.

Please consider the attached materials in support of the precautionary case for pediatric acetaminophen warnings and informed consent.

Document 1 presents a Bayesian weight-of-evidence analysis of the evidence discussed in the citizen petition. The purpose of this analysis is to evaluate the cumulative strength of evidence across multiple independent lines of inquiry rather than relying on any single study design in isolation. The overall pattern of evidence, including epidemiology, animal models, mechanistic data, biomarker studies, and related disease associations, supports concern regarding neurodevelopmental risk in susceptible children.

Document 2 discusses the biomarker-based evidence on prenatal acetaminophen exposure and why these studies should be given substantial weight when interpreting the larger body of prenatal epidemiology. Biomarker-based designs help reduce problems associated with maternal recall bias and exposure misclassification that may affect retrospective survey-based studies. These findings strengthen the argument that observed associations in prenatal acetaminophen research may reflect genuine biological effects rather than statistical artifact alone.

The final document addresses the overlap between autism and asthma and their potential connection to acetaminophen exposure. This line of evidence is relevant because it suggests the possibility of shared underlying mechanisms involving oxidative stress, glutathione depletion, immune dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammatory signaling. Importantly, it also supports the broader concern that acetaminophen-related effects may extend beyond traditional liver toxicity models and involve systemic developmental and immunologic pathways.

Taken together, these materials further support the need for precautionary pediatric warnings and more complete risk communication to parents and clinicians regarding potential developmental and systemic risks associated with acetaminophen exposure during vulnerable periods of childhood development.

title: Comment from Anonymous
printtext:
Please see the attached supplemental comment and supporting references regarding the limitations of sibling-control analyses in prenatal neurodevelopment research.

Recent literature suggests that sibling comparison designs may attenuate or obscure true associations in certain contexts involving developmental exposures, particularly where exposure misclassification, carryover effects, shared environmental susceptibilities, epigenetic mechanisms, or bias amplification may be present. These concerns are directly relevant to the interpretation of prenatal acetaminophen studies, where several large maternal recall studies employing sibling-control methodologies have been treated as disproportionately determinative in evaluating risk.

Importantly, the recently published JAMA study by Ahlqvist et al. (2024) on prenatal acetaminophen exposure and neurodevelopmental outcomes demonstrated substantial attenuation of associations in sibling analyses despite strong associations in population-level analyses, while contemporaneous methodological literature has cautioned that sibling-control methods may themselves introduce important bias under certain conditions. Additional large-scale prenatal neurodevelopment studies, including Madley-Dowd et al. (2024), similarly emphasize that sibling comparisons should be interpreted as one methodological tool among many, rather than as definitive evidence against causality.

Accordingly, these materials are submitted in support of the Americans for Scientific Integrity citizen petition requesting pediatric precautionary labeling for acetaminophen. At minimum, the evolving methodological literature suggests that null sibling-control findings should not be treated as dispositive when evaluating the overall weight of evidence regarding potential neurodevelopmental risk.

title: Comment from Americans for Scientific Integrity
printtext: Petitioner respectfully submits for inclusion in the administrative record the following newly published study: Herrington et al. (2026), “Two-Hit Exposure to Lipopolysaccharide and Acetaminophen Alters Larval Zebrafish (Danio rerio) Swim Behavior.”  This experimental study is notable because it directly models a “two-hit” framework in which early-life inflammation is followed by acetaminophen exposure, a sequence that closely mirrors real-world pediatric use, where acetaminophen is most commonly administered during fever, infection, or other inflammatory states. The authors report that acetaminophen exposure altered neurobehavioral outcomes in developing zebrafish and, importantly, that combined exposure to inflammation and acetaminophen produced interaction effects on behavior that were not fully explained by either exposure alone, including changes in activity and lateralized movement patterns. While the findings are modest, derived from an animal model, and do not establish causation in humans, the study is highly relevant from a regulatory perspective because it addresses a key limitation of the existing literature: most prior studies evaluate acetaminophen in isolation rather than in the biologically realistic context in which it is actually used. The authors themselves emphasize that this context is critical, noting that inflammation and illness are independently associated with neurodevelopmental risk and may interact with drug exposure. Accordingly, this study provides additional mechanistic and experimental support for the plausibility of a context-dependent risk model, in which acetaminophen exposure during periods of immune activation may have different developmental effects than exposure in a non-inflamed state. Petitioner does not contend that this study is dispositive on its own, but rather that it strengthens the overall evidentiary record by demonstrating that inflammatory context is not merely a confounder but may be an integral component of risk. For this reason, the study is directly relevant to the requested pediatric warning and should be included in the FDA’s evaluation of whether current labeling adequately reflects real-world conditions of use and potential susceptibility in early childhood.

title: Comment from Anonymous
printtext:
This comment is submitted in support of the request for a precautionary neurodevelopmental warning regarding acetaminophen use in infants and young children, including acetaminophen exposure beginning on the first day of life.
Attached is a PDF copy of Tylenol and Autism: Evidence, Scientific Blunders, and Medicine Gone Wrong by William Parker, PhD. The book is highly relevant because it collects and organizes evidence concerning acetaminophen exposure during early brain development, including neonatal exposure, immature infant metabolism, oxidative stress, susceptibility, laboratory animal evidence, human epidemiologic evidence, and the absence of adequate long-term neurodevelopmental safety testing for pediatric use.
This comment is not intended to ask FDA to rely on the book itself as dispositive evidence. Rather, the attached volume serves as a source guide, index, and synthesis of the underlying scientific literature, with citations to original studies provided in the notes section beginning on page 225.
Several sections are particularly relevant. Chapter 5, beginning on page 81, addresses the timing of acetaminophen-associated neurodevelopmental risk and explains why the period immediately after birth and the first years of life may be especially important. Pediatric acetaminophen exposure can begin in the hospital, during the immediate postnatal period, when drug metabolism, detoxification capacity, and brain vulnerability may differ materially from older children and adults.
Pages 85-90 are especially relevant to immature neonatal metabolism. Parker discusses evidence that newborns and young infants may not metabolize acetaminophen in the same way as older children and adults, and that the ability to process acetaminophen safely may change substantially during early life. This is central because long-standing assumptions about pediatric acetaminophen safety have often been based on liver injury endpoints, not long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes.
Pages 91-95 discuss case histories and the Schultz findings concerning regression into autism following early-childhood acetaminophen exposure. These sections address pediatric exposure after birth, including repeated dosing during illness, vaccination-related fever or pain, and other common childhood circumstances in which acetaminophen may be administered.
Chapter 6, beginning on page 97, summarizes laboratory animal evidence relevant to developmental neurotoxicity, including multiple studies reporting persistent behavioral, cognitive, social, auditory, or neurodevelopmental effects following early-life acetaminophen exposure. Pages 139-142 are especially important because they discuss recent work concerning N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), the toxic metabolite of acetaminophen, and preliminary evidence of acetaminophen-related adduct formation in neonatal brain tissue. This evidence is directly relevant to biological plausibility and to whether the developing brain has been adequately protected by current pediatric labeling.
Chapter 7, beginning on page 113, addresses additional evidence bearing on pediatric safety, including the history of assumptions that acetaminophen was safe for babies and children, the weakness of the evidence base supporting that assumption, and the difference between evidence of safety and the absence of adequate neurodevelopmental safety testing.
Appendix B, pages 189-194, provides concise evidence summary tables organizing pharmacologic, epidemiologic, laboratory animal, and other lines of evidence. These tables may be useful to FDA as a roadmap for reviewing the underlying literature cited throughout the book.
The central regulatory issue is not whether every mechanism has been fully resolved, but whether current labeling adequately communicates the uncertainty and potential neurodevelopmental risk during the most vulnerable periods of pediatric brain development.
For these reasons, the attached book should be included in the administrative record and considered as a source guide and synthesis relevant to the requested pediatric neurodevelopmental warning for acetaminophen use in infants and young children.

title: Comment from Anonymous
printtext:
I am submitting the attached 2026 study by Aslan et al., Plasma Metabolic Features Associated with Developmental Regression in Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Pilot Untargeted Metabolomics Study, because its findings may be relevant to the mechanistic questions raised in this petition.
The investigators compared children with regressive autism, children with non-regressive autism, and typically developing controls. Among the most notable findings, the feature putatively identified as prostaglandin E3 (PGE3) was reduced 7.13-fold in the regressive autism group compared with controls, versus only 1.58-fold in the non-regressive group. The study also identified marked differences involving DHEA-S, sialylated glycoconjugates, glycoprotein metabolism, and sphingolipid/myelin pathways. Several of these biochemical systems intersect pathways relevant to acetaminophen biology. Acetaminophen directly affects cyclooxygenase/prostaglandin signaling, while acetaminophen disposition in infants and young children depends substantially on sulfation, making the findings involving prostaglandin metabolism and the sulfated neurosteroid DHEA-S particularly worthy of further investigation.
This study did not measure acetaminophen exposure and therefore does not establish that acetaminophen caused these metabolic abnormalities. Its relevance is that it identifies significant biochemical differences associated specifically with developmental regression, including abnormalities in pathways that overlap with known acetaminophen pharmacology. In evaluating the totality of evidence concerning acetaminophen exposure during early neurodevelopment, FDA should consider these findings alongside the experimental, mechanistic, pharmacologic, and epidemiologic evidence already submitted to the record.

title: Comment from American Public Transportation Association
printtext:
Full Letter is attached.

Ms. Veronica Vanterpool
Deputy Administrator
Federal Transit Administration
Washington, DC 20590

Re: Notice of Proposed Buy America Waiver for Battery Electric Minibuses and Request for Comment (Docket No. FTA-2024-0018)

Dear Deputy Administrator Vanterpool:

The American Public Transportation Association (APTA) represents a $79 billion industry that directly employs 430,000 people and supports millions of private-sector jobs. Our members include more than 340 US public transit agencies, many of which provide public transportation services using vans and minivans.

We greatly appreciate the opportunity to respond to the Federal Transit Administration’s (FTA) Notice of Proposed Buy America Waiver for Battery Electric Minibuses and Request for Comment (Docket No. FTA–2024-0018), published in the Federal Register at 89 FR 104285 on December 20, 2024.

APTA strongly supports Buy America and applauds the Administration’s continued efforts to ensure the use of American-made materials in FTA-funded projects. These Buy America requirements are critical to U.S. job creation, timely project delivery, quality, and building U.S. manufacturing capacity.

To help achieve these Buy America goals, APTA strongly supports the phased three-year general non-availability waiver of Buy America requirements proposed by FTA for battery electric minibuses used in public transportation.
 
On November 18, 2024, FTA issued a five-year partial, time-limited general unavailability waiver of Buy America for vans and minivans because FTA was unable to identify any manufacturer of non-Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA)-accessible vans and minivans that fully complies with Buy America. APTA had urged and fully supported that waiver. The proposed waiver for battery electric minivans used in public transportation is appropriate and important for the same reason: the unavailability of Buy America-compliant electric vehicles. Approximately 150 letters have been submitted to FTA in support of the waiver. Granting the waiver will enable public transportation agencies to procure electric minivans, providing safe and climate-friendly transportation to thousands of transit riders.

APTA members deploy minivans for on-demand, paratransit, and carpool services. The use of electric minivans helps transit agencies meet state zero-emission and climate mandates and supports important community efforts to provide non-polluting transit vehicles. The use of larger zero-emission buses to serve on-demand and paratransit needs typically is neither economical nor operationally feasible. Electric minivans are sized to serve these smaller, highly specialized markets in an environmentally friendly manner. Unfortunately, as FTA has concluded, there simply are no electric minibuses available in the United States that meet FTA’s domestic content or final assembly requirements under Buy America.

APTA was very fortunate to participate with FTA and the members of the Administration at the White House Clean Bus Manufacturing Roundtable held in February 2024. Through the APTA Bus Manufacturing Task Force, we have worked together with bus manufacturers, suppliers, and public transit agencies to build a more competitive, financially stable bus manufacturing capacity in this country. These efforts are critical as the nation’s transit agencies transition to zero-emission bus technologies. Unfortunately, more work is required to ensure that all types of zero-emission buses—from heavy duty buses to minivans—can be manufactured in the U.S. in compliance with Buy America.

The proposed phased waiver will provide a two- to three-year cushion for building U.S. capacity to manufacture electric minivans, while preserving the ability of transit agencies to meet their immediate needs for such minivans. Moreover, the procurement of minivans now will help demonstrate to manufacturers and suppliers that there is a strong and long-term market in the United States for U.S.-manufactured and US-assembled buses and bus components. APTA, of course, strongly encourages foreign minivan manufacturers to incorporate American-made and compliant parts and components that are readily available and would not adversely impact delivery requirements.

Thank you for your consideration and support for public transportation in the United States.

Sincerely,

Paul P. Skoutelas
President and CEO

We are responding to requested comments on the Federal Transit Administration’s (FTA) proposed general non-availability waiver of Buy America requirements for electric minibuses, which was recently published for public input. Hoekstra Transportation strongly opposes this proposed waiver and urges the FTA to review its implications.

Under the Buy America statute, federally funded rolling stock projects must meet stringent domestic content and assembly requirements, ensuring that U.S.-manufactured vehicles are prioritized.
As a dealer for Optimal Low-Floor EV, a Michigan based company, the S1 low-floor electric shuttle is fully compliant with these standards, and this proposed waiver would not only undermine these established principles but also negatively impact our business and the broader domestic manufacturing sector.

4. Market Saturation by Non-Compliant Imports:
The waiver’s broad scope and its application to any eligible FTA funding recipient risk saturating the market with non-compliant imports, limiting opportunities for compliant manufacturers to grow and innovate.

We believe that granting this waiver would set a concerning precedent, weakening the Buy America statute’s intent, and adversely affecting U.S. manufacturers and workers.

While I recognize the urgency of addressing supply constraints, I would like to raise several critical considerations about the scope and potential impacts of this Buy America waiver for battery electric minibuses.

Given the basis of the waiver is the lengthy timelines to receive Buy America-compliant vehicles, it is essential for the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) to determine what quantity of production would normalize these timelines. 2. The proposed three-year duration is meant to foster domestic manufacturing; however, there is no assurance that this period will yield the intended results. Instead, it is possible that the influx of vehicles produced using cheap offshore labor could shutter existing domestic manufacturing capacity. This would leave the market dependent on foreign suppliers, potentially necessitating a longer-term or even permanent waiver, which would be counterproductive to the goals of Buy America.

3. The waiver provides no binding assurances that foreign suppliers will establish manufacturing facilities in the United States to create a level playing field. Without firm commitments or clear penalties for failing to establish domestic operations, the waiver could fail to achieve its stated purpose of encouraging onshoring. I urge the FTA to impose conditions that require foreign suppliers to establish U.S.-based production facilities within the waiver period to qualify for future contracts.

title: Comment from Valley Regional Transit
printtext:
Valley Regional Transit (VRT) is the regional public transportation authority for Ada and Canyon counties in Idaho. VRT serves two individual urbanized areas: one large urban area encompassing Boise, Meridian and the surrounding area with an urbanized population of 449,776, and one small urban area encompassing Nampa, Caldwell and the surrounding area with an urbanized population of 193,935 as reported from the last census. VRT’s full urbanized population is 643,711, and the service area (two-county region) population is approximately 822,890.

VRT relies on federal funding for a portion of all rolling stock and is therefore obligated to meet Buy America standards for all purchases. VRT has a strategic goal of reducing our carbon footprint through the use of electric and low-emission vehicles. We are currently working to set a target for achieving that goal for all our rolling stock.

VRT’s transit fleet (full-size) is currently a mix of Battery Electric Buses (BEB) and Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) buses. These buses are designed for transit use with a low floor entry design and a longer useful life than body-on-chassis vehicles. The transit fleet is used for high volume fixed route service.

VRT has a paratransit fleet of body-on-chassis vehicles and large transit vans. Some of these have been converted to CNG propulsion, while others are gasoline powered. We have not been able to find smaller battery electric vehicles that meet current standards. Additionally, none of our paratransit fleet has low-floor entry and the useful life of the vehicles is a shorter span than our transit fleet. Our paratransit fleet is used on lower volume fixed routes as well as various demand response services including paratransit and microtransit services.

VRT desires to transition the entire fleet, both transit and paratransit, to low and no emission vehicles to achieve our energy goals. In order to meet that target, we are interested in procuring zero emission battery electric minibuses that also meet our other goals of low floor entry and longer useful life. We are confident that battery electric unibody low floor vehicles will improve the energy efficiency, accessibility, comfort and rider experience on our lower volume routes and VRT’s many demand response services.

VRT researched vehicles available for procurement that meet FTA's domestic content or final assembly requirements for Buy America eligibility and have been unable to find a domestic manufacturer of electric minibuses who meet our criteria. VRT is one of the agencies that signed on to support the non-availability request for waiver for electric minibuses.

We ask FTA to finalize and grant a three-year non-availability waiver of FTA's Buy America rolling stock requirements for any vehicle with all of the following characteristics.
•Powered by a battery electric propulsion system
•Has, or is capable of having, low-floor entry
•Is of unibody or monocoque construction
•Has a gross vehicle weight rating or weight of less than 11,794 kg (26,001 lbs)
•Is designed to transport fewer than 16 seated passengers including the driver
•Is not required to report to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration under the American Automobile Labelling Act

VRT is confident that such a waiver will encourage potential market entrants to build the requisite domestic supply chains and establish a final assembly facility in the United States, and we hope it will spur domestic manufacturers to compete in this market. VRT understands that that the waiver would phase out over time and end three years after it is finalized.

Please grant the waiver as proposed.
